result:
The kitchen at ten on a Wednesday is a small country. The overhead light is that slightly yellow, tired thing that makes everything look a half-second older than it is. The refrigerator hums its one low note, the only music anyone is hearing. A glass of water sits in the sink, and you've been meaning to wash it for forty minutes, and you'll mean to wash it for forty more.

The window is fogged at one corner where your breath touched it, and you could trace a letter in the condensation. You don't. You just watch a single drop start down the glass, slow as a decision being made, and then stop, and then start again.

Outside, a neighbor's dog barks at nothing, or at a moth, or at the particular frequency of the streetlight. The sound comes and goes with no argument. It is not a complaint. It is just a fact of the night, the same way the hum is a fact of the kitchen. You don't fix it. You let it be the texture of the hour.

This is the part of the evening nobody writes about, and that's the point. No one is performing. The dishes are still in the sink. The day has already been a small, unremarkable thing, and tonight is going to be a small, unremarkable thing, and that smallness is not a failure. It is the shape of a life that is not on fire. And in the not-on-fire there is a strange, quiet permission to just stand at the counter, press your palm flat against the cool tile, and breathe in the smell of dish soap and old coffee, and let the nothing of it be enough.

It is enough. It has been enough all along.
